notes: REQ-003 / TASK-003 (issue #290). Written as a proposal; applied by REQ-004 / TASK-005 (issue #292). Its rows are now the one source for supabase/seed/010_exercise_definitions.sql, supabase/migrations/20261001000019_catalog_section_repair.sql and docs/backend/rollback/catalog-section-repair.sql: change a row here, then run npm run seed and npm run gr:repair. ambiguous entries are not applied, whatever they recommend, until they become rows.
Reviewed, not generated. src/test/generation-reliability/section-mapping-ledger.test.ts holds it to the capture, the seed and the cited sources.
REQ-005 / TASK-004 (issue #291) adds the Minimal-tier main-work rows: primary_lift and canBePrimary for eight exercises that need nothing but the athlete's own body. Applied with the rest.

One row per exercise whose section membership or primary eligibility changes. before is the pre-change capture; after is before plus the proposed tags. Every row here is additive: no tag is removed, and canBePrimary changes only from false to true, only on a row that adds primary_lift.

Evidence is kind:value. component and role are the reviewed workout-anatomy tags in docs/backend/evidence/previous-migrations/00031_tag_exercises.sql; legacy-anchor and cue are the pre-change capture; name is the exercise name; equipment is an entry in the exercise's seeded equipment_options; ref is an entry in references, whose quote must be present in its path.

The rule for a primary_lift row: the owner's decision that Minimal main work is low/no-equipment training, plus the section's own description (squats, deadlifts, presses), plus three catalog facts that agree — a reviewed component that is the squat, hinge or press pattern itself, the old catalog's primary anchor for the same pattern, and bodyweight among its equipment options with nothing in its name or cues that asks for a bar, a bench or an anchor point. An exercise the catalog lists as bodyweight but that needs apparatus (pull-ups, chin-ups, inverted rows, dips) is under ambiguous with a recommendation to leave: retrieval filters on equipment_options, so tagging it would offer it where the apparatus does not exist.
The primary_lift rows are not Minimal-only. Each of them is offered as main work at every tier, beside the loaded lifts already there; nothing is removed from any tier.

The rule for a row is the section's own onboarding description plus an independent catalog fact that agrees with it. skill_power: a jump or an Olympic lift or pull by name, tagged triple-extension. carries: a carry by name, in the reviewed stability batch headed 'anti-motion core, carries'. stability_balance: tagged single-leg-stability and not an Olympic lift.

ambiguous lists the exercises where the evidence points both ways, each with a recommendation. A recommendation of add is the default disposition unless the owner overrides it; it takes effect only by becoming a row, because the seed may not differ from the capture without one.
An exercise absent from both lists has no evidence for any of the three sections and is not proposed.

Every carry needs dumbbells or kettlebells, so carries stays empty at the Minimal tier under this proposal. That is not a reason to tag something that is not a carry: docs/process/generation-reliability/configuration-dispositions.json records the selection as prevented at the preference boundary, with its reason, and every other legal configuration as supported.

onboarding.skill_power.quote: Explosive movements — jumps, throws, Olympic lifts

onboarding.carries.quote: Loaded carries — farmer’s walks, suitcase carry

onboarding.core.quote: Rotational and stability work for your midsection

onboarding.primary_lift.quote: The main heavy movement — squats, deadlifts, presses

decision.minimal-main-work.quote: Bodyweight, calisthenics, plyometrics, bands, and similarly appropriate work should form a useful workout. Minimal is not a degraded barbell program and should not disable ordinary Goals merely because no heavy implement exists.

decision.minimal-primary-gap.quote: the repaired taxonomy/preset must support meaningful main work without treating a barbell lift as the only possible session anchor.

journal.bodyweight-primary-gap.quote: every primary lift in the seeded catalog needs a barbell, dumbbell, kettlebell or bar.

anatomy.knee-flexion.quote: Knee bending under load. Underlies squats, lunges, step-ups.

anatomy.hip-hinge.quote: Hip-dominant flexion/extension with neutral spine. The motion underlying deadlifts, RDLs, swings.

anatomy.horizontal-press.quote: Forward pressing pattern. Underlies bench press, push-ups, dips.

anatomy.role-compound-lift.quote: Multi-joint loaded movement that can serve as a primary lift. | Deadlift, back squat, bench press, pull-up.

anatomy.role-activation.quote: Light bodyweight exercise that trains a specific primitive for movement prep.

anatomy.triple-extension.quote: Simultaneous extension of hips, knees, ankles. Underlies all power movements (clean, snatch, jump).

anatomy.landing-mechanics.quote: Absorbing force with control. Trained by box step-downs, controlled jump landings.

anatomy.cardio-output.quote: Trained by general conditioning work (jumping jacks, jump rope, light rowing).

anatomy.single-leg-stability.quote: Unilateral lower-body balance. Trained by single-leg RDLs, split squats, balance work.

anatomy.grip.quote: Forearm and hand endurance under load. Trained by dead hangs, farmer carries, heavy holds.

anatomy.anti-lateral-flexion.quote: Resisting sideways bending. Trained by side planks, suitcase carries.

anatomy.role-stability.quote: Movement that trains anti-motion qualities (brace, anti-rotation, anti-lateral-flexion). | Planks, Pallof presses, suitcase carries.

anatomy.role-conditioning.quote: Full-body or sustained-effort movement that builds work capacity. | Burpees, mountain climbers, rowing intervals.

A jump, which the section description names first, cued as explosive. Tagged triple-extension and anchored to power in the old catalog. It needs no equipment.
An Olympic lift, which the section description names. The anatomy spec's own example of a power movement is the clean; the tags and the old power anchor agree.
An Olympic lift variation started from the hang. Tagged triple-extension, anchored to power, cued as explosive.
The full Olympic clean. Tagged triple-extension and anchored to power in the old catalog.
An Olympic lift variation. The anatomy spec's own example of a power movement is the snatch; the tags and the old power anchor agree.
The dumbbell or kettlebell snatch: the Olympic movement with a single implement. Tagged triple-extension and anchored to power. It is the section's Olympic-style lift where there is no barbell.
The jerk is the second half of the Olympic clean and jerk. Tagged triple-extension and anchored to power.
The competition jerk. Tagged triple-extension and anchored to power. Its single-leg-stability tag is handled under ambiguous.
An Olympic pull. The reviewed tags file it under Power accessories, give it triple-extension, and the old catalog anchored it to power.
An Olympic lift drill. The reviewed tags file it under Power accessories, give it triple-extension, and the old catalog anchored it to power.

The high pull is the Olympic pull taken to the elbows-high finish, here with a kettlebell or dumbbell. Tagged triple-extension and cued as explosive. The old catalog anchored it to pull rather than power, which the name and the tag outweigh: it is the same movement as clean-pull.
The section description names it: farmer's walks. A carry by name, in the reviewed batch headed carries, and the anatomy spec's example for grip.
The section description names it. A carry by name, in the reviewed batch headed carries, and the anatomy spec's example for both anti-lateral-flexion and the stability role.
A loaded carry by name, in the reviewed batch headed carries.
A loaded carry by name (Front Rack Carry), in the reviewed batch headed carries.

rows.rationale: Stability: single-leg work by name, and the anatomy spec's first example for single-leg-stability. Its own cue is about balance. Main work: the section description names deadlifts, and this is the one hip-hinge in the catalog that needs no implement — tagged hip-hinge, the primitive the anatomy spec says underlies deadlifts and RDLs, anchored to hinge in the old catalog, with bodyweight among its equipment. On one leg, bodyweight is a real load. It is the Minimal tier's hinge.
Single-leg work by name, tagged single-leg-stability. Keeping the hips level on one leg is the control the section is for, and it needs no equipment.

Main work: the section description names squats; this is a squat by name, tagged knee-flexion, anchored to squat in the old catalog, with bodyweight among its equipment. With the rear foot raised nearly all of the athlete's weight is on one leg, which makes it the heaviest squat available without an implement.

ambiguous.rationale: For: tagged triple-extension, anchored to power in the old catalog (as its secondary anchor, behind press), cued as a dip and drive — the jerk's leg drive without the catch. Against: it is not a jump, a throw or a competition Olympic lift, and it is primarily a press. Recommend adding: two independent catalog tags call it a power movement and the addition takes nothing away from primary_lift.

For: tagged triple-extension and anchored to power as its primary anchor in the old catalog, so the old power day already served it. Against: a squat into a press is none of the description's jumps, throws or Olympic lifts. Recommend adding, on the strength of the primary power anchor.
The dumbbell form of thruster with the same tags and the same primary power anchor. Recommend the same disposition as thruster, whichever way that goes.

For: tagged triple-extension and cued as a hip snap, a ballistic movement. Against: the old catalog anchored it to hinge only, and it is not a jump, a throw or an Olympic lift. Recommend adding: the reviewed tag is the later and more specific judgement, and it gives the section a kettlebell-only option.

For: every rep ends in a jump cued as explosive, it is tagged triple-extension, and the old catalog anchored it to power. Against: its role is conditioning and the anatomy spec uses it as the example of conditioning work, so it is usually programmed for work capacity rather than power. Recommend adding: it stays in conditioning, and with squat-jumps it is the only no-equipment candidate the section would have.

For: the reviewed tags file it under Power accessories and the old catalog anchored it to power as its primary anchor; it is an Olympic-lifting skill drill, and the section is Skill / power. Against: it is slow and strict, with no triple-extension tag — skill, not power. Recommend adding, as the skill half of the section.

For: the old catalog anchored it to power as its primary anchor, and it is an Olympic-lifting assistance lift. Against: the reviewed tags give it hip-hinge and no triple-extension and file it with the heavy compound lifts, not under Power accessories; nothing in it is explosive. Recommend leaving it out: a slow strength pull is what the section description excludes.

For: it is a jump by name and tagged landing-mechanics. Against: no triple-extension tag, no power anchor, its role is cardio, and the anatomy spec uses it as the example of sustained cardio-output. Recommend leaving it out: it is low-amplitude and sustained, not explosive.

For: it is loaded locomotion, and two of its three cues are word for word overhead-carry's. Against: it is a lunge by name, the reviewed tags file it under Squat accessories with single-leg-stability, and it is not in the batch headed carries. Recommend leaving it out of carries; a row adds it to stability_balance.

For: loaded locomotion, which coaches often programme beside carries, and it would give the section a candidate that needs no dumbbell or kettlebell. Against: the load is pushed, not carried; its role is conditioning; it is not in the batch headed carries; and the catalog lists its equipment as bodyweight although it needs a sled, so tagging it would offer it where no sled exists. Recommend leaving it out.

evidence: cue:Hand over hand or backward drag
ambiguous.rationale: The same case as sled-push: loaded locomotion, but dragged rather than carried, tagged conditioning, and listed as bodyweight although it needs a sled. Recommend leaving it out.

For: it is the only single-leg-stability exercise the rows do not add, because it is caught in a split stance. Against: it is a maximal Olympic lift that can be the session's primary lift; the stance is how the bar is received, not what is trained. Recommend leaving it out of stability_balance; a row adds it to skill_power.

For: its reviewed role is stability, and the section is labelled Stability / balance. Against: the role means anti-motion trunk work, which the Core description already claims (rotational and stability work for your midsection) and where the exercise already sits; the Stability / balance description is single-leg work and proprioception. Recommend leaving it in core only.
The same case as side-plank: role stability, but trunk anti-rotation that Core already describes and already holds. Recommend leaving it in core only.
The same case as side-plank: role stability, but trunk bracing that Core already describes and already holds. Recommend leaving it in core only.

For: its reviewed role is compound_lift, the anatomy spec names the pull-up as an example of a movement that can serve as a primary lift, and it would give the Minimal tier a pull. Against: it hangs from a bar, as its own cues say, yet the catalog lists bodyweight among its equipment — so retrieval offers it to anyone, bar or not. Tagging it primary_lift would make a bar-dependent exercise Minimal main work, which REQ-005 rules out. Recommend leaving it until its equipment says pullup_bar only; that correction is outside this ledger, which records section membership and primary eligibility, and once made the exercise is a sound primary_lift row for the Home tier and above.
The same case as pull-ups: role compound_lift, but done from a bar while listed as bodyweight. Recommend the same disposition as pull-ups, whichever way that goes.

For: a multi-joint bodyweight pull, and the Minimal tier has no pulling main work. Against: its cue is to pull the chest to a bar, the reviewed tags file it under Pull accessories, and the catalog lists it as bodyweight although it needs something to hang under. Recommend leaving it out for the same reason as pull-ups.

For: a heavy calisthenic press, which the anatomy spec names beside push-ups, tagged with both pressing primitives. Against: it is done between parallel bars or on a dip station, which the catalog does not record — it lists bodyweight only — and the Minimal preset has no such apparatus. Recommend leaving it out; push-ups and decline-push-ups carry the Minimal press.

For: it is the squat itself, the first movement the section description names, and it needs nothing. Against: its reviewed role is activation — light bodyweight movement prep — it sits in warmup and conditioning, and the capture records it as the regression of split-squat. It is what the main work is rehearsed with, not the main work. Recommend leaving it out; the split squats and lunges are the Minimal squat pattern under real load.

evidence: cue:Use hands to push back up
ambiguous.rationale: For: one of the hardest bodyweight posterior-chain movements, anchored to hinge in the old catalog. Against: the reviewed tags give it posterior-chain-activation and no hip-hinge — it is a knee-flexion curl for the hamstrings, single-joint — and the feet have to be held down by something the catalog does not record. Recommend leaving it as an accessory.

For: a squat by name, tagged knee-flexion, bodyweight only. Against: its own cue calls it quad isolation, and a movement that isolates one muscle is the opposite of the section's main movement. Recommend leaving it as an accessory.
